item.text: {"decisions":[{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:cursor:301c1497d14b1ed17100","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"Usable as Cursor’s primary evidence that Rollouts and Security Reviewer became available on Teams and Enterprise plans, with concrete workflow scope: named telemetry integrations, an editable pre-merge monitoring plan, pre/post-deploy comparison, configurable pause/revert actions, and enumerated security checks. These capabilities are highly relevant to small teams lacking dedicated release or security staff and are a novel extension from code generation into post-PR controls. Cursor sells the plans, however, and supplies no sample, false-positive rate, incident outcome, security test set, or independent comparison. Claims that the bots reliably distinguish intended effects, catch regional regressions, or find and fix vulnerabilities therefore remain unverified and cannot establish production readiness. It overlaps thematically with OpenAI review automation and Sourcegraph’s autonomous-codebase vision but is a separate underlying announcement, not corroboration. Use Piece 01 for the availability change, Piece 02 to test its reliability claims against independent evidence, and Piece 03 to motivate a bounded pilot with human approval and measured false positives, misses, and rollback outcomes." ,"version_id":"v-9e5e5fac9d48014feb9c5bfc"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:cursor:84d2e8f0655374a11ab2","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"This is useful vendor operational evidence that agent-harness design—not just model choice—can alter cost: Cursor reports trimming about 66% of its system prompt, dynamically loading infrequently used tools, a 46.9% token reduction specifically among sessions that called an MCP tool, and an overall 7% user-cost reduction without measured quality loss. The A/B-testing description is more inspectable than a bare marketing assertion and is directly relevant to small teams managing long-running-agent expense. Nevertheless, Cursor benefits commercially from portraying its harness as efficient, and the excerpt omits sample sizes, test dates, model mix, confidence intervals, the quality metric, and the baseline for several figures. Token use, cost, latency, and tool errors are efficiency/activity measures, not accepted-code quality or maintenance outcomes. This is a distinct harness-engineering report, not a duplicate of Cursor’s bot launch. Use Piece 01 for the newly reported context-management changes, Piece 02 for the bounded vendor measurements and missing denominators, and Piece 03 for the practical implication that teams should measure local cost and quality together." ,"version_id":"v-5fed8f79222f91b61985792d"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:github:7a6dc2d18f9ec533b042","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"GitHub is authoritative for the narrow availability facts: Gemini 4 Argon is entering a gradual Copilot rollout for specified plans, uses provider-list usage pricing, and can be governed through administrator model policies, including default enablement. Those access, cost, and governance changes matter to small teams. GitHub and Google have commercial incentives to promote the model, and the performance language is not usable as effectiveness evidence: no benchmarks, scores, task definitions, baselines, model settings, or edge-case measure support “solved more tasks” or “thoroughly checks its work.” The item is novel as a model-distribution and policy change, not proof of production readiness, and is independent of the Cursor and OpenAI announcements. Use Piece 01 for what became available, Piece 02 to show which performance claims do not survive inspection, and Piece 03 to recommend explicit model-policy review and repository-specific evaluation before enabling a new default." ,"version_id":"v-9e3b7675dd5b66ce334d1e75"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:independent-research-authors:258392c93310baab1471","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"AgentSWE offers unusually relevant original evidence: 25 commissioned tasks across creation, editing, and optimization; limited illustrative cases during development; frozen submissions; held-out acceptance cases; requirement-derived rubrics; and hard gates or source-benchmark objectives. That method directly tests the gap between a plausible demonstration and delivered behavior, and the reported trajectories—visible-case overfitting, hollow runtimes, and unsupported completion claims—are actionable verification risks for small teams. The authors created the benchmark and may favor the framing it exposes; the excerpt also lacks model-by-model scores, artifact details, and uncertainty, while 25 agent-building tasks cannot establish performance on ordinary product work. It is a new independent benchmark rather than a reaction to any vendor launch. Use Piece 02 as a strong counterweight to vendor capability claims and Piece 03 to support held-out acceptance tests, runtime checks, and evidence-backed definitions of done." ,"version_id":"v-b8c088105e97e9e6f3ce9ed9"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:independent-research-authors:337cbc4cedf5cfb1d758","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"Accept narrowly as an argumentative synthesis, not as independent verification of every study it cites. Its useful contribution is the explicit juxtaposition of differently scoped findings: a reported 26% task-completion increase across 4,867 developers, a 16-developer randomized trial covering 246 mature-repository tasks that reported 19% longer completion time, and a 2,755-repository difference-in-differences study separating aggregate output from core-contributor review and rework. This helps the target audience see why task boundedness, codebase maturity, seniority, and outcome choice may explain apparent disagreement. The original studies and their full baselines are not supplied here, so the numbers may only be presented as this paper’s attributed summaries, not independent corroboration. The authors are advancing a strong thesis that software engineering is indispensable; categorical claims such as a limitation that “no amount of training” can eliminate exceed the shown support. Its novelty is synthesis rather than a new experiment, and it overlaps with InfoQ’s requirements-and-verification discussion without depending on it. Use Piece 02 to organize conflicting measurements and Piece 03 for the bounded implication that teams should persist specifications, domain constraints, and verification artifacts." ,"version_id":"v-e9b1abf6d3b4b6aeda723cc0"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:independent-research-authors:89ac63769de00fed6835","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"This supplies original qualitative evidence about supervision: observations and workflow diagrams from 19 experienced developers were used to construct a seven-stage framework, then applied to public Reddit discussions. The reported practices—front-loading planning, assigning some supervision to other agents, and converting recurring guidance into reusable assets—are directly relevant to small teams organizing delegated work and offer a novel connected-process lens. The sample is small and selected, the Reddit material is not an independent outcome validation, and the study measures how supervision is organized rather than whether it reduces defects, time, or rework. No commercial product incentive is evident, although the authors have an incentive to demonstrate the utility of their framework. It is independent of the product announcements and complements rather than corroborates the Matt Pocock demonstration. Use Piece 02 to define the supervisory work hidden behind autonomy claims and Piece 03 to derive a staged, reviewable delegation workflow while acknowledging the absence of causal outcomes." ,"version_id":"v-9bde3907428df8ef68a78026"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"feed:sourcegraph:32584b6ceadae8f3a512","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The September 14 publication falls outside the mechanical 30-date window ending October 15, so neither the launch nor the historical Batch Changes figures can support this edition. Even apart from freshness, the relevant new claim is a Sourcegraph product announcement aimed mainly at hundreds or thousands of repositories, making it less representative of a 2–20-person team. Sourcegraph sells the featured product, and the excerpt provides no completion rate, CI-pass rate, review burden, defect outcome, cost baseline, or independent customer evaluation for Agentic Batch Changes; the 2,200-change example concerns the predecessor system. Its script-versus-agent orchestration is potentially novel, but the in-window autonomous-codebase essay covers the forward-looking concept without making this stale announcement fresh. This rejection is editorial and date-specific, not a judgment that the product is globally unreliable." ,"version_id":"v-b33c45204054589dffdd9e18"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:sourcegraph:ea3179ffe2d4c95b4f7b","piece_ids":["03"],"reason":"Accept only as a clearly labeled vendor design thesis for the watch list. The concrete, usable contribution is its proposed architecture of event triggers, production signals, callable investigation or coding functions, and human notifications—a potentially consequential shift from human-initiated prompt-to-PR work toward continuous maintenance. That architecture is relevant to small teams considering what controls future agents will require, although the essay is oriented toward very large brownfield codebases. Sourcegraph sells code-search and batch-change tooling, and its assertions that prompt-to-PR is essentially solved, model quality has plateaued, or brownfield maintenance is completely unsolved are anecdotal and unsupported by measurements. It does not establish that an autonomous codebase exists in production. The thesis overlaps with Cursor Rollouts’ production-triggered workflow but is independent in origin and cannot corroborate Cursor’s effectiveness. Use only in Piece 03 as a watch signal, with its commercial incentive and speculative status explicit." ,"version_id":"v-1c7d0d28b27050f0e12c26c2"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"podcast:infoq:5925e1fbf36f4960a85e","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"The named, transcripted interview is usable as attributed practitioner judgment about ambiguous requirements, explicit tests, legacy systems whose true requirements are unclear, and the unresolved choice between incremental modification and regeneration. Those observations are pertinent to hands-on leads and provide a useful boundary between low-consequence internal tools and systems needing careful specification and validation. The conversation supplies no study, incident, measured review outcome, or representative sample, so claims that requirements are the gating factor or code review is ineffective cannot be stated as general facts. The guest and publisher benefit from attention, though no direct featured-tool sales incentive is shown. The themes overlap with the research synthesis and AgentSWE, but the interview is an independent practitioner perspective rather than corroborating evidence. Use Piece 02 to contrast expert judgment with measured evidence and Piece 03 for bounded requirements-and-test practices, not production-readiness conclusions." ,"version_id":"v-fa6a1a051450d1962bb56646"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"podcast:infoq:5950b2ca18b6b0b75291","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The topics—psychological safety, ownership of generated output, verification overload, and junior development—are audience-relevant, but this excerpt provides broad prescriptions without a concrete team example, incident, observational method, outcome measure, or precise limitation. “Psychological safety is essential” and the asserted urgent need for advanced telemetry are expert opinions rather than inspectable evidence. The guest and podcast have attention incentives, and the material offers limited novelty relative to the stronger InfoQ requirements interview and the independent supervision study; because it comes from the same InfoQ series, it would not add an independent publisher or corroboration. Reject for this evidence portfolio as duplicative and insufficiently supported, not because psychological safety is unimportant or the speaker is generally unreliable." ,"version_id":"v-dbe33bbe448ee0d2555a358e"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"podcast:infoq:d6cf9bc155dcb06cf247","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The September 14 publication is outside the mechanical 30-date window ending October 15. Its preceptorship proposal and warning about architecture are potentially relevant practitioner ideas, but the excerpt supplies no training outcomes, organizational example, comparison group, or measure supporting them. It also overlaps with the two newer InfoQ conversations about junior training and human oversight, so it would add neither freshness nor an independent distribution channel. The named guest reduces attribution uncertainty but does not overcome the date or evidentiary limits; the podcast and guest also benefit from attention. Reject for this edition rather than treating a later repost or continued relevance as a new event." ,"version_id":"v-6e820812bb6374c9491cabb4"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"youtube:9yPyoxlyc5Q","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"This provides a concrete practitioner demonstration in an actual course-video-manager repository: GitHub issues externalize work, a worktree isolates it, a reusable skill explores through a subagent, and the agent asks specific questions about hierarchy selectors and empty plans before implementation. That named example is useful evidence of how requirement elicitation can be operationalized for a small team, although it is only one creator’s workflow and reports no time, defect, acceptance, or maintenance outcome. The presentation occurs at a GitHub Copilot event and promotes both Copilot and the speaker’s highly visible skills repository, creating platform and attention incentives. Its reusable pre-work pattern is more novel and concrete than generic prompting advice. It overlaps conceptually with the supervision study but is independent practitioner observation, not outcome corroboration. Use Piece 02 as a bounded workflow example and Piece 03 as a pilotable practice whose effect should be measured locally." ,"version_id":"v-ab01f07d4890bf0557ad681d"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"youtube:hTAWHgQI4xg","piece_ids":[],"reason":"This is a broad concepts tutorial rather than production evidence. The opening pilot anecdote is not documented, and the claim that the presenter’s team now completes work that once took weeks or months in minutes lacks task definitions, baselines, sample size, accepted outcomes, or maintainability follow-up. IBM’s educational channel has a commercial incentive to portray agent adoption as an inflection point. Spec-driven development and the shift from implementing to conducting are relevant but not novel here and duplicate better-supported observations in AgentSWE, the supervision study, and the InfoQ interview. Reject because the usable claims are generic or unsupported, not because every conceptual recommendation is necessarily wrong." ,"version_id":"v-470d183469c7db5d35e05d67"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"youtube:7XzjQa8z0uc","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The item explicitly targets beginners and demonstrates Codex through a toy cookie-shop game, putting it outside Agent Signal’s production-engineering scope. It offers a walkthrough of projects, Git, multiple agents, skills, and cloud handoff but no production repository, acceptance criteria, security controls, CI outcome, defect measure, rework, cost, or maintenance evidence. The creator benefits from tutorial attention, and any product-availability facts are derivative of OpenAI’s own materials, which are present in this evidence set. Its novelty is instructional packaging rather than a new capability or practitioner finding. Reject as generic beginner content and duplicative product coverage." ,"version_id":"v-aa6fb499336c3701ec05174c"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"youtube:IZXv6a78NDw","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"OpenAI’s demonstration is primary evidence for the narrow product facts that GitHub code review is generally available, GitLab support is in preview, permissioned cloud reviews can run automatically, review comments can appear beside the change, and users can invoke a separate local review with team instructions, skills, and connectors. The integrated review inbox and cloud/local workflow are a consequential and relevant capability change. OpenAI sells Codex, however, and supplies no review latency, defect-detection precision or recall, comment acceptance, rework, rollback, or maintainer-satisfaction measure. The title claim that code review is “no longer the bottleneck” therefore does not survive scrutiny. This independently overlaps with Cursor’s automated security review but is a separate product announcement and does not corroborate its accuracy. Use Piece 01 for availability, Piece 02 to separate workflow scope from the unsupported outcome claim, and Piece 03 to recommend a human-owned pilot measuring review usefulness and misses." ,"version_id":"v-aa6fb499336c3701ec05174c"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"youtube:PUBc2G0Tj5E","piece_ids":["01","03"],"reason":"The vendor demo is usable to establish the announced workflow scope of the new Codex CLI: a full-screen task interface, concurrent tasks, navigation among agents, follow-ups, conversation forks into worktrees, remote control, voice input, usage analytics, and rendered diagrams. These coordination features are relevant to small teams experimenting with parallel agents and are a distinct development from OpenAI’s code-review release. OpenAI has a direct commercial incentive, and the toy burrito projects demonstrate interface behavior rather than production effectiveness. The excerpt gives no exact version, rollout constraints, plan eligibility, task-success rate, coordination overhead, cost, review burden, or accepted outcome, so it cannot support productivity or production-readiness claims. Use Piece 01 for the coordination-surface change and Piece 03 as a watch signal for whether multi-agent interfaces expose enough status, isolation, and human intervention controls." ,"version_id":"v-f95ed73f67d6b610264834f4"},{"decision":"defer","item_id":"youtube:J9NQTYUP6k0","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The video attributes changing advice to a Claude Code creator’s Hacker News comment and YC talk, but the supplied evidence does not expose those primary passages, their dates, full context, or applicable product versions. “Top 1%” is undefined, and the claims that plan mode is no longer useful, planning now happens adequately during execution, and post-hoc diagrams can replace up-front review have no task sample or outcome comparison. The creator benefits from attention and packages secondhand advice as a ranked workflow, while much of the definition-of-done guidance duplicates the more inspectable Pocock demonstration and independent supervision research. This could become useful if the direct posts or timestamped talk segments, exact Claude versions, and observed before/after outcomes are supplied; until then it should not be used as either practitioner corroboration or a current capability claim." ,"version_id":"v-8bb3472c3858254a3ab9d00e"}]}
